cases-L1#0.why: Hurricane case studies are really about telling a hurricane from other disasters. Each name on this list is a tropical storm that grew over warm ocean and then hit land. The big harm came from wind, storm surge, and rain together. Galveston 1900 is the deadliest U.S. natural disaster on record, from surge before warnings existed. Later storms show how forecasts and building rules changed outcomes.
cases-L1#0.pic: Draw a simple U.S. map with the Gulf and Atlantic coasts. Put a dot for each place: Galveston, New Orleans (Katrina), New York and New Jersey (Sandy), Houston area (Hilary is West Coast, so draw it near Southern California). Label each dot with its year.
cases-L1#0.analogy: Think of a list of famous football games. You do not replay every play, you just remember the game, the year, and why it mattered. Here the 'game' is a storm and 'why it mattered' is the damage type. The analogy stops working because storms are natural and no team plans them.
ways: Hurricane list means the event was a tropical cyclone, not a blizzard or tornado outbreak.
Galveston 1900, Andrew 1992, Katrina 2005, Sandy 2012, Ida 2021, Ian 2022, Hilary 2023, Helene 2024, Erin 2025, Melissa 2025. That is 10 names, spanning 125 years.
Name plus year plus 'ocean storm with surge' = hurricane case.

ex.q: Hurricane Katrina (2005) caused major flooding in which U.S. city?
steps: Katrina is on the hurricane list, so think Gulf Coast.
Recall the surge and broken levees (flood walls) in 2005.
The levees failed in New Orleans, Louisiana.
Check: flooding came from surge, a hurricane hazard.

cases-L1#0.trap: Mixing up the lists. Students put Storm of the Century (1993) with hurricanes because it sounds huge. Ask: did it form over warm tropical ocean? If it is a winter storm, it goes on the other list.
cases-L1#0.tip: Hurricanes on the first list all had a name or came from the sea: Gal-Katrina-Sandy-Ida-Ian.

cases-L1#1.why: These events are big weather disasters that were not hurricanes. Each has a different cause, so the type tells you the clues. A blizzard needs wind and snow. A drought needs weeks of no rain. A tornado outbreak needs lots of warm, humid, sheared air. Knowing the cause lets you name the event from data without memorizing every detail.
cases-L1#1.pic: Make a 6-row chart. Left column: event name and year. Right column: one picture word, like snowflake, dust cloud, funnel, rain cloud, river, big winter storm. Draw a tiny icon for each.
cases-L1#1.analogy: Like sorting school supplies into bins: pencils, glue, markers. Each event goes in its own bin by what it is made of. The analogy stops because real events can mix, such as a storm with both snow and flooding.
ways: Blizzard 1888 = snow and wind. Dust Bowl = drought. Xenia 1974 = tornado.
1888, 1930s, 1974, 2011, 1993, 1993: six events from three centuries' worth of eras (1800s and 1900s and 2000s).
Ask: what fell or blew? Snow, dust, wind funnel, rain, river water.

ex.q: The Storm of the Century (March 1993) was a huge winter storm. Which type of event is it?
steps: It is on the non-hurricane list.
It brought heavy snow, high wind, and cold to the eastern U.S.
So it is a winter storm, not a tropical cyclone.

cases-L1#1.trap: Thinking 'Storm of the Century' means a hurricane. The name is just a nickname. The type comes from the clues: cold air, snow, and wind.
cases-L1#1.tip: B-D-X-A-G-S: Blizzard, Dust, Xenia, April, Great flood, Storm.

cases-L1#2.why: The rules give you data and ask you to analyze it. So you do not need a dictionary of dates. You only need to know what kind of event each one was. A type tells you what the data should look like: wind speeds for hurricanes, snow depth for blizzards, rainfall for floods.
cases-L1#2.pic: Draw a funnel. Wide top says 'event data'. Middle says 'clues'. Narrow bottom says 'type of event'.
cases-L1#2.analogy: A detective does not memorize every crime, just the patterns. Clues point to a kind of crime. Here clues point to a kind of storm. The analogy stops because detectives need proof, and weather data gives probabilities.
ways: Know the type of each event, not the story.
Wind 130 mph = hurricane Cat 4. Snow 24 inches with 40 mph wind = blizzard.

ex.q: A report shows months of heavy rain and the Missouri and Mississippi rivers over their banks in 1993. What type?
steps: List the clues: months of rain, two big rivers.
Heavy rain over a long time points to flooding.
Rivers rising is a river flood, not a flash flood.
Match to the list: Great Flood of 1993.

cases-L1#2.trap: Memorizing every date and detail. Practice spotting clues instead.

cases-L2#0.why: This is a four-step habit for any case question. Naming the storm type narrows what scale or tool applies. Clues tell you what data matter. The right scale gives a rating. The date matters because scales changed: the Fujita scale before 1 Feb 2007 and the Enhanced Fujita after. Skipping the date check is how people choose the wrong scale.
cases-L2#0.pic: Draw four boxes in a row with arrows: Type, Clues, Scale, Date. Put a small calendar icon on the last box.
cases-L2#0.analogy: Like a recipe: pick the dish, check ingredients, use the right pan, check the oven temperature. Each step prevents a different mistake. It stops working because recipes are fixed and storms vary.
ways: Name it, list clues, pick the scale, check the date.
Tornado on 2011-04-27: 2011 is after Feb 1, 2007, so use EF. Tornado on 1974-04-03: before, so use F.

ex.q: A tornado hit on 3 April 1974 with peak wind estimated 170 mph. Which scale applies, and what is the rule?
steps: Step 2: clue is wind damage estimate.
Step 3: tornado scales are F or EF.
Step 4: 1974 is before 1 Feb 2007, so use the original Fujita scale.

cases-L2#0.trap: Using EF for old tornadoes. Always compare the date to 1 Feb 2007 first.
cases-L2#0.tip: Name, Clues, Scale, Date: N-C-S-D, 'Never Check Stale Dates'.

cases-L2#1.why: The Dust Bowl was not a single storm. Drought dried the soil. Farmers had plowed up the native prairie grass whose roots held the dirt. With no roots and no rain, strong winds lifted the soil into huge dust storms. Cause: drought plus bare, plowed ground plus wind. Remove any one and it would have been much milder.
cases-L2#1.pic: Draw a flat field with no plants. Draw wavy arrows lifting brown specks into a tall brown wall. Add a dry sun above.
cases-L2#1.analogy: A bare table dusted with flour: blow and it flies. If you cover it with a cloth (grass), it stays. Mapping: flour is topsoil, cloth is grass roots, your breath is wind. It stops working because the Dust Bowl lasted years across many states.
ways: Long dry spell plus loose soil plus wind equals dust storms.
Years of drought in the 1930s. Rain near 0 for months means soil moisture near 0, so soil is loose.

ex.q: Which historic event was mainly a long drought with massive dust storms on the Plains?
steps: Clue: dust storms on the Plains.
The event is the Dust Bowl.

cases-L2#1.trap: Calling it a hurricane or tornado because dust walls look like storms. Check for drought first.

cases-L2#2.why: In 1993 the Midwest got rain for months, not just one big storm. Soil filled up, so extra rain ran straight to rivers. The Mississippi and Missouri rose over banks and levees for weeks. Cause: a long wet pattern with storm after storm over the same region. Because the pattern lasted so long, it is a river flood, not a flash flood.
cases-L2#2.pic: Draw two rivers joining on a map of the Midwest (Missouri from the west, Mississippi down the middle). Shade a wide blue band along them.
cases-L2#2.analogy: A sink with the tap on and a clogged drain. The tap is steady rain and the sink is the river basin. It overflows slowly. It stops working because rain also soaks into soil first.
ways: Months of heavy rain made big rivers flood.
1993 summer: rain on top of full soil. If 2 in/week falls for 8 weeks, that is 16 in on already wet ground.
River floods take days to weeks.

ex.q: The Great Flood of 1993 mainly affected which river basins?
steps: Recall the cause: months of heavy rain.
Rain was over the central U.S.
Rivers draining that area are the Mississippi and Missouri.
Floods were along those rivers and their tributaries.
Answer: upper Mississippi and Missouri river basins.

cases-L2#2.trap: Calling it a flash flood. A flash flood takes minutes to hours. This took weeks.

clouds-L1#0.why: Cumulonimbus is the only cloud that makes thunderstorms. Warm moist air rises strongly, cools, and keeps growing upward until it hits the stable layer (the tropopause) and spreads into an anvil. Because the updraft is so deep and strong, it can carry hail, build charge for lightning, and make strong winds. That is why it can bring every type of severe weather.
clouds-L1#0.pic: Draw a tall tower with a flat anvil top and a dark flat base. Put arrows going up in the center, and rain and hail falling from the base.
clouds-L1#0.analogy: A boiling pot with a lid on: steam rises hard, hits the lid, and spreads sideways. The pot is the ground, steam is the updraft, the lid is the stable layer, the sideways steam is the anvil. It stops working because the atmosphere has no actual lid.
ways: Cb tops can pass 12 km (about 40,000 ft) while bases sit near 1 to 2 km.

ex.q: Which cloud is the thunderstorm cloud?
steps: Names: cumulus (puffy), nimbus (rain), so cumulo-nimbus is puffy plus rain.
Stratus is a flat layer and cirrus is thin, high ice.
Only cumulonimbus is tall and makes lightning.

clouds-L1#0.trap: Picking cumulus. Cumulus is fair-weather puffs. The 'nimbus' part means rain.

clouds-L1#1.why: A wall cloud forms where rain-cooled air gets pulled into the updraft. That air is humid, so it condenses at a lower height than the rest of the cloud base. The result is a lowered section. If it rotates and is beneath the main updraft, the storm is organizing rotation near the ground. That is why it is a key warning sign for a tornado.
clouds-L1#1.pic: Draw a big flat cloud base. Under one spot, draw a lower block hanging down like a step. Add a curved arrow showing it turning.
clouds-L1#1.analogy: A tent with one pole pushed up from underneath so the fabric droops down beside it. Mapping: the updraft is the pole, the lowered cloth is the wall cloud. It stops working because a wall cloud rotates and fabric does not.
ways: Wall cloud: lowered, often rotating base under the main updraft.
Normal base 1,500 m. Wall cloud base may sit 300 to 500 m lower.
Lowered AND rotating AND under the updraft = take cover.

ex.q: A lowered, often rotating cloud base under the main updraft is a what?
steps: Find the location: under the updraft, not at the edge.
It is lowered from the normal base.
Not a shelf cloud, which is at the front edge.

clouds-L1#1.trap: Mixing wall and shelf clouds. Wall: under the updraft, may rotate. Shelf: along the front edge, does not rotate.
clouds-L1#1.tip: A WALL stands where the storm breathes IN.

clouds-L1#2.why: A shelf cloud forms where the storm's cool outflow slides under warm moist air. The warm air is forced up fast and condenses, forming a wedge. The cool air racing out is the gust front. So the shelf marks the leading edge of strong winds. It looks scary but is not rotating like a wall cloud.
clouds-L1#2.pic: Draw the ground and a storm to the right. Draw a long low wedge-shaped cloud pointing left with an arrow showing cold air rushing out.
clouds-L1#2.analogy: A snowplow shoving snow ahead of itself. Mapping: the plow is the cool air, the pushed snow is warm air lifted into cloud. It stops working because snow is not warm.
ways: Shelf cloud: wedge on the leading edge, marks the gust front.
Gust front winds can reach 58 mph or more in severe storms.

ex.q: A wedge-shaped low cloud on a storm's leading edge usually marks what?
steps: Leading edge: the front of the storm.
Cool outflow edge is the gust front.
So the shelf cloud is over the gust front.

clouds-L1#2.trap: Calling it a tornado sign. Shelf clouds mean wind, not a funnel.

clouds-L2#0.why: A funnel cloud is a rotating cone of condensed water droplets. Low pressure in the spinning air cools it, so water vapor condenses into a visible cone. If it does not touch the ground, it is not called a tornado. If it touches, it is. A thin funnel can quickly reach the ground, so treat it seriously.
clouds-L2#0.pic: Draw a storm base. Hang a pointed cone from it. Stop the tip in the air. Draw a ground line below. Then draw the tip touching to show a tornado.
clouds-L2#0.analogy: A spinning top balanced on your finger: the spin is the rotation, the finger is the ground. Not touching = funnel cloud. Touching = tornado. It stops working because real funnels are air, not solid.
ways: Funnel cloud = rotating cone not touching the ground.
Funnel cloud: 0 ft contact. Tornado: ground contact at 1 ft or more of debris/damage.

ex.q: A rotating cone-shaped cloud hanging from a storm but not touching the ground is a what?
steps: No contact means not a tornado yet.

clouds-L2#0.trap: Calling every funnel a tornado. Contact with ground is the test.
clouds-L2#0.tip: Funnel in the air, tornado on the ground.

clouds-L2#1.why: Mammatus are pouches that hang under an anvil. Sinking air is cooler than the air around it, and it sinks in lumps. The lumps hold cloud droplets, so they show as pouches. They often show up when the storm is weakening, but the storm can still be dangerous. They are not a tornado sign.
clouds-L2#1.pic: Draw a big flat anvil. Under it draw rows of round bumps like cow udders or bubble wrap, hanging down.
clouds-L2#1.analogy: Bubbles of bubble wrap or sagging balloons under a table. Mapping: each balloon is a sinking lump of cloud. It stops working because balloons are filled, but mammatus are made of sinking air.
ways: Each pouch is about 1 to 3 km wide and lasts about 10 minutes.

ex.q: Pouch-like cloud shapes under an anvil are called what?
steps: They hang from the anvil base.
Not wall clouds, which are lower rotating blocks.

clouds-L2#1.trap: Thinking mammatus mean a tornado is coming. They do not. They show sinking air.
clouds-L2#1.tip: MAMMA-tus look like MAMA's soft pouches.

dh-L1#0.why: Drought is not just no rain today. It is a long stretch of less moisture than normal. First rain runs short (meteorological). Then soil dries and crops suffer (agricultural). Then streams and reservoirs run low (hydrological). Each type builds on the one before. Water takes time to drain, so reservoirs show the problem last.
dh-L1#0.pic: Draw three stacked boxes: sky with no rain, field with dry cracked soil, river with low water. Arrows go down from one to the next.
dh-L1#0.analogy: A bank account. Rain is income, soil is your wallet, reservoir is savings. If income stops, the wallet empties first, savings last. It stops working because savings can be refilled quickly if a big storm hits.
ways: Drought: far too little precipitation for a long time.
If normal is 4 in/month and you get 1 in/month, you are short 3 in each month; after 6 months, 18 in short.

ex.q: Name the type of drought when streams, lakes, and reservoirs run low.
steps: Streams and reservoirs hold water on the surface.
Low water bodies point to the third type.
Check: it shows up last in a long drought.

dh-L1#0.trap: Mixing up the types. Agricultural is about soil and crops. Hydrological is about rivers and reservoirs.
dh-L1#0.tip: Hydro = water you can see in rivers.

dh-L1#1.why: A heat wave is a long run of unusually high temperatures. Heat is most dangerous when nights stay warm, because your body does not get a break to cool down. Humid air adds to it, because sweat evaporates more slowly. Cities hold heat in pavement and buildings. The danger comes from body heat piling up day after day.
dh-L1#1.pic: Draw a thermometer line across 5 days. Show daytime highs as peaks and nights as valleys that stay above 75 F. Add a person under a hot sun.
dh-L1#1.analogy: A phone that never gets to charge. Daytime heat drains you. Cool nights recharge you. Hot nights mean no recharge. It stops working because bodies cannot be plugged in.
ways: Hot days plus hot nights give the body no recovery.
Day 1 high 100, low 80. Day 2 high 102, low 82. Body never drops below stress.
Warm nights make heat waves deadly.

ex.q: Overnight temperatures stay high during a heat wave. Why is this dangerous?
steps: Normally nights cool the body and buildings.
If it stays hot, no cooling happens.
Risk of heat illness rises, especially for kids and older adults.
Answer: the body cannot recover, so heat stress adds up.

dh-L1#1.trap: Thinking only the afternoon high matters. The night low matters too.

dh-L1#2.why: A blocking ridge is a big area of high pressure that stalls. Sinking air under a high warms and dries, so clouds do not form. The ridge also acts like a rock in a stream, pushing storms around it. Under the ridge it stays sunny and hot, and soil dries. Dry soil heats faster, so the heat strengthens the ridge.
dh-L1#2.pic: Draw a big H on a map. Draw storm arrows bending around it. Under the H, write 'sinking, dry, hot'.
dh-L1#2.analogy: A big rock in a river. Water flows around it, leaving a calm spot behind. The rock is the ridge, water is storms. It stops working because rock is solid and the ridge changes over days.
ways: A stalled high pushes storms away and gives sinking, dry air.
A ridge may sit for 7 to 14 days. 14 days with no rain is a drought start.

ex.q: Which pattern often causes both drought and heat waves?
steps: Look for something that stops rain and adds heat.
If it stalls, it is blocking.

dh-L1#2.trap: Linking drought to low pressure. Lows bring rising air and clouds.
dh-L1#2.tip: High and dry, low and wet.

dh-L1#3.why: Drought and heat hurt in four ways. Crops lack water and fail. Cities limit water use. Dry plants and soil burn easily, so wildfires spread. Bodies overheat, causing cramps, exhaustion, and heat stroke. All four trace back to too little water and too much heat. Drinking water helps because sweat is your body's cooling system.
dh-L1#3.pic: Draw four icons around a sun: wilted plant, faucet with an X, flame, and a sweating person.
dh-L1#3.analogy: A car engine overheating. Water is the coolant, heat is the work. Low coolant means breakdown. It stops working because you can drink more water but a car cannot.
ways: Crop loss, water limits, fire risk, heat illness.
On a hot day you can lose over 1 liter of sweat per hour; drink often, not just when thirsty.
Drink water before you feel thirsty.

ex.q: What should you drink more of during a heat wave?
steps: Choose water, not sugary or caffeinated drinks.

dh-L1#3.trap: Waiting until thirsty. Thirst shows up late.

hurr-L1#0.why: Hurricane, typhoon, and cyclone are the same kind of storm. The names are just location labels. Atlantic and Northeast Pacific: hurricane. Northwest Pacific: typhoon. Indian Ocean and South Pacific: cyclone. A spinning ocean storm with warm core is what they all are. Only the map region changes the word.
hurr-L1#0.pic: Draw a world map with three colored zones: Atlantic and east Pacific (hurricane), west Pacific (typhoon), Indian Ocean and southern oceans (cyclone).
hurr-L1#0.analogy: Soda is called 'pop', 'soda', or 'coke' depending on where you live. Same drink, different words. Mapping: the drink is the storm, the word is the region. It stops working because soda names are slang, while storm names are official.
ways: Same storm, different names by ocean.
Winds at 74 mph or more qualify in every ocean for hurricane-strength.

ex.q: A hurricane, a typhoon, and a cyclone are what?
steps: Check what stays the same: the physics.
Answer: the same type of storm (tropical cyclone).

hurr-L1#0.trap: Thinking typhoons are stronger. They are not a different type.

hurr-L1#1.why: A tropical storm system grows in steps as winds speed up. An invest is a disturbance being watched. Depression is under 39 mph. Tropical storm is 39 to 73 mph and gets a name. Hurricane is 74 mph or more. Major hurricane is Category 3 and up, 111 mph or more. More wind means more damage because force grows faster than wind speed.
hurr-L1#1.pic: Draw a staircase going up. Label steps with Invest, TD, TS (39-73), Hurricane (74+), Major (111+).
hurr-L1#1.analogy: Leveling up in a video game. Each level needs more points (wind). It stops working because storms can also skip levels or fall back.
ways: Under 39: depression. 39-73: tropical storm. 74+: hurricane. 111+: major.

ex.q: A tropical storm has winds of 65 mph. How many mph more are needed to be a hurricane (74 mph)?

hurr-L1#1.trap: Subtracting from 73. Hurricane is 74 and up.
hurr-L1#1.tip: 39 and 74: 'Thirty-nine, seventy-four, the storm gets a name and then a roar.'

hurr-L1#2.why: The Saffir-Simpson scale sorts hurricanes by sustained wind into five categories. It rates wind only, not surge or rain. Each step up brings much more damage because wind force grows faster than wind speed, roughly with its square. A Cat 5 can destroy homes.
hurr-L1#2.pic: Draw five bars rising like a bar chart. Under each write the category and mph: 74-95, 96-110, 111-129, 130-156, 157+.
hurr-L1#2.analogy: A bike speed scale: walk, jog, run, sprint, rocket. Each speed hits harder. It stops working because storms also differ in size and rain.

ex.q: A hurricane has sustained winds of 105 mph. Which category?
steps: Find where 105 fits in the ranges.

hurr-L1#2.trap: Rounding up to the next category. Use the ranges exactly.

hurr-L2#0.why: A hurricane is a heat engine. Warm ocean water gives heat and moisture. At 26.5 C or warmer, evaporation is strong enough to feed the storm. Low wind shear lets the storm stack straight up. Away from the equator is needed because the Coriolis force (spin from Earth) is too weak there to start rotation.
hurr-L2#0.pic: Draw a bowl of warm ocean. Arrows rise from it. Add a vertical column showing calm winds aloft. Mark the equator with an X where spin is missing.
hurr-L2#0.analogy: A campfire needs wood, air, and a spark. Missing one and it dies. Mapping: warm water is the wood, low shear is steady air, Coriolis is the spark. It stops working because a fire is chemical.
ways: Warm water, moisture, low shear, away from equator.

ex.q: A hurricane needs warm ocean water. About what temperature, in C, is the minimum?
steps: Colder water gives too little fuel.
So the minimum is about 26.5 C.

hurr-L2#0.trap: Thinking 20 C is enough. It is not.

hurr-L2#1.why: A hurricane has parts with different jobs. The eye is the calm center where air sinks. Around it the eyewall has the strongest wind and rain because air rises hard there. Spiral bands farther out bring showers and sometimes tornadoes. So the worst weather is the ring around the calm, not the calm itself.
hurr-L2#1.pic: Draw a circle target. Center: eye, calm. First ring: eyewall, worst. Spirals outward: bands.
hurr-L2#1.analogy: A donut. The hole is the eye, the dough is the eyewall, sprinkles are the bands. It stops working because donuts are not rotating.
ways: Calm eye, fierce eyewall, bands with showers and tornadoes.
Eye width is often 20 to 40 miles.

ex.q: Spiral bands in a hurricane can sometimes produce what?
steps: Spin in the bands can make small tornadoes.

hurr-L2#1.trap: Thinking the eye is the most dangerous. It is calm, but the eyewall around it is not.

hurr-L2#2.why: Storm surge is water pushed onshore by wind. Big storms push more water. Slow storms push longer. Shallow coasts let water pile up higher. Surge is often the deadliest hazard because water is heavy and floods homes fast. It is not a tide, and it is not rain.
hurr-L2#2.pic: Draw a side view of a coast sloping gently. Draw wind arrows pushing a wave of water up the slope and over a house.
hurr-L2#2.analogy: Blowing on a bowl of soup: the soup piles on one side. Mapping: your breath is wind, the soup is the sea. It stops working because real surge also includes low pressure.
ways: Wind pushes ocean water onto land.
Cat 4 surge can reach 13 to 18 ft above normal tide.
Strong + big + slow + shallow = high surge.

ex.q: Storm surge is what?
steps: Surge is a rise in water level.
It is caused by wind pushing water.
It is not rain or tide.
Answer: water pushed onshore by a storm's winds.

hurr-L2#2.trap: Confusing surge with rain flooding. Surge comes from the sea.

hurr-L2#3.why: Hurricanes weaken when fuel runs out or something tears them apart. Land cuts off warm water and adds friction. Wind shear tilts the storm. Dry air dries it out. Cooler water gives less heat. Without moisture and heat from the ocean, the engine stalls.
hurr-L2#3.pic: Draw a hurricane over water and then over land. Add an X on the arrow from the ocean to the storm when over land.
hurr-L2#3.analogy: A car running out of gas. Land is an empty tank. It stops working because a hurricane may still drop heavy rain after losing wind.
ways: Winds can drop 25 percent within about 24 hours over land.

ex.q: How does a hurricane weaken over land: it loses its supply of what?
steps: So moisture and heat are cut.
Answer: warm, moist ocean air (moisture and heat).

hurr-L2#3.trap: Thinking weakening means no danger. Rain and flooding can last.

light-L1#0.why: Charge forms where ice and graupel (soft hail pellets) collide inside the cloud. Light ice crystals get carried up and end up positive. Heavier graupel falls and ends up negative. So the top is mostly positive and the middle and base are mostly negative. Lightning is the discharge that evens it out.
light-L1#0.pic: Draw a tall cloud. Put plus signs near the top, minus signs near the bottom. Draw rising arrows with tiny ice crystals and falling arrows with big pellets.
light-L1#0.analogy: Rubbing a balloon on hair. Rubbing moves charge. Mapping: balloon is graupel, hair is ice. It stops working because the cloud has billions of particles.
ways: Collisions separate charge. Top positive, base negative.
Cloud potential can reach millions of volts.
Light goes up (+), heavy goes down (-).

ex.q: Where is the main positive charge in a typical thunderstorm?
steps: Answer: in the upper part of the cloud.

light-L1#0.trap: Thinking the base is positive. It is mostly negative.

light-L1#1.why: Lightning is named by where it goes. Cloud-to-ground hits the earth. Intracloud stays inside one cloud. Cloud-to-cloud jumps between clouds. Cloud-to-air shoots into clear air. Most flashes stay in the cloud because the opposite charges are closer inside the cloud than the ground.
light-L1#1.pic: Draw two clouds. Draw four bolts: one to the ground, one inside a cloud, one between clouds, one out the side into the air.
light-L1#1.analogy: Sparks between objects. A spark jumps the shortest path. It stops working because lightning picks branches.
ways: Four types: CG, IC, CC, CA.
About 75 percent of flashes do not reach the ground.
Most lightning never reaches the ground.

ex.q: Most lightning flashes stay where?
steps: Opposite charges are within the cloud.
Short path inside the cloud is easiest.
So most flashes stay in the cloud.

light-L1#1.trap: Thinking most lightning hits the ground. Most does not.

light-L1#2.why: Light reaches you almost instantly. Sound travels about 1 mile in 5 seconds. So the gap between flash and thunder tells distance. Divide seconds by 5 for miles. It is an estimate, not exact.
light-L1#2.pic: Draw a bolt and a person. Draw a line between them with a clock showing seconds. Write 5 s = 1 mi.
light-L1#2.analogy: A stadium: you see the pitcher throw, then hear the bat crack later. Mapping: light is sight, sound is the delay. It stops working because it is not exact in wind.
ways: 30 seconds or less means go inside.

ex.q: The flash-to-bang time is 10 seconds. About how many miles away is the lightning?
steps: Sound travels about 1 mile per 5 seconds.

light-L1#2.trap: Dividing by 3 (that is for kilometers). Miles use 5.

light-L1#3.why: Lightning sends out a radio pulse. Sensors at different places hear it at slightly different times. Computers use the time differences to find where it came from. More sensors give better accuracy. It is like triangulation.
light-L1#3.pic: Draw three towers around a dot. Draw circles from each tower that cross at the dot.
light-L1#3.analogy: Three friends hear a shout at different moments and can work out where it came from. It stops working because lightning is far faster.
ways: Time differences between sensors locate strikes.
Radio travels about 300,000 km per second, so timing must be in microseconds.

ex.q: Lightning detection systems find strikes mainly by what?
steps: Answer: timing the signal at several sensors.

light-L1#3.trap: Thinking they use cameras only. Radio timing is the main method.

maps-L1#0.why: A station model packs a whole weather report into a small space. Every number has a fixed spot, so you read it like a form, not a picture. Temperature sits upper left, dew point lower left, pressure upper right, pressure change lower right. The circle in the middle shows how much sky is covered, and the staff shows the wind. Fixed spots let hundreds of stations fit on one map.
maps-L1#0.pic: Draw a small circle. Write T at upper left, Td at lower left, P at upper right, change at lower right. Draw a line (staff) out of the circle for wind.

precip-L1#0.why: In warm clouds there is no ice. Cloud droplets are tiny and float. Bigger ones fall faster, hit smaller ones, and merge. This is collision-coalescence. As they grow they fall faster and gather more, until they are heavy enough to fall as rain. It needs a tall, wet cloud.
precip-L1#0.pic: Draw a big drop falling through a bunch of tiny dots, swallowing them and getting bigger.

precip-L1#1.why: In cold clouds, both ice crystals and supercooled droplets (liquid below 0 C) exist. Air has more vapor than ice needs, and less than droplets need. So vapor leaves droplets and sticks on ice. Ice crystals grow while droplets shrink. When the crystals get heavy they fall.
precip-L1#1.pic: Draw a small crystal with tiny droplets around it. Draw arrows from droplets to the crystal. Make the crystal bigger.
precip-L1#1.analogy: A playground where one kid hogs the toys. The crystal hogs the water vapor. It stops working because toys are not made of gas.
ways: Crystal grows from 0.1 mm to over 1 mm while droplets evaporate.

precip-L1#1.trap: Thinking both grow. The droplets shrink.
precip-L1#1.tip: Bergeron: ice gets big, drops go away.

precip-L1#2.why: Two ways to grow ice. Riming: supercooled drops hit ice and freeze on contact, making graupel and, in strong updrafts, hail. Aggregation: ice crystals bump and stick, which makes snowflakes. Snowflakes are clumps of crystals. Aggregation works best near 0 C where crystals are sticky.
precip-L1#2.pic: Draw a pellet with small bumps from frozen drops (riming). Draw a snowflake made of several joined crystals (aggregation).
precip-L1#2.analogy: Riming is paint spraying on a wall. Aggregation is gluing stickers together. It stops working because ice is not sticky like glue.
ways: Riming adds frozen drops. Aggregation sticks crystals.
Hail grows in many layers, each layer from a rimed drop trip.
Riming makes graupel and hail, aggregation makes snow.

torn-L1#1.why: Tornadoes need warm, humid air and a spinning storm. In spring, warm Gulf air meets cold air from the north over the Plains. Late afternoon is when the ground is hottest, so air is most unstable. The Plains and Southeast get the most. But the ingredients can appear any month, so tornadoes are possible any time.
torn-L1#1.pic: Draw a U.S. map. Shade the Plains and Southeast. Draw a clock showing 4 to 6 pm.
torn-L1#1.analogy: A pot of water reaching a boil after a while. Heating takes time, so the peak comes late. It stops working because storms need lift too.
ways: Spring, late afternoon, Plains and Southeast, but any time.
Peak hour is about 4 to 6 pm local time.
Hot afternoon, warm moist air, danger.

ex.q: What time of day do tornadoes most often occur?
steps: Hottest time is mid to late afternoon.

torn-L1#1.trap: Believing tornadoes only happen in spring afternoons.

torn-L1#2.why: The EF scale rates a tornado by the damage it causes, then gives an estimated wind speed. EF0 is 65 to 85 mph, EF1 86 to 110, EF2 111 to 135, EF3 136 to 165, EF4 166 to 200, EF5 over 200. Because rating comes after the fact, it is an estimate. Each step means worse damage.
torn-L1#2.pic: Draw six steps going up. Label each with EF number and range.
torn-L1#2.analogy: Like grading a test after it is done. It stops working because the tornado does the damage, not the grade.
ways: EF3 and up is violent-ish, EF4 and EF5 are devastating.

ex.q: A tornado's estimated peak wind is 160 mph. What is its EF rating?

torn-L1#2.trap: Picking EF4 because 160 feels high. Use the ranges.

torn-L2#0.why: The original Fujita (F) scale was used before 1 Feb 2007. The Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale started on that date. Both rate tornado damage, not the wind directly. EF uses more damage indicators and updated wind estimates. So date decides.
torn-L2#0.pic: Draw a timeline with a line at Feb 1, 2007. Label F on the left and EF on the right.
torn-L2#0.analogy: A video game patch: before the patch the old rules, after the new ones. It stops working because the scale did not replace history.
ways: F before, EF on or after.

ex.q: Which scale is used for tornadoes occurring after February 1, 2007?

torn-L2#1.why: A hook echo is a shape on radar reflectivity where rain and hail wrap around the rotating part of a supercell (the mesocyclone). It looks like a fishhook. It shows that the storm is rotating. A tornado is often near the tip of the hook.
torn-L2#1.pic: Draw a blob of radar color with a curved tail wrapping around a small circle at the lower right.
torn-L2#1.analogy: Cream swirled into coffee. It stops working because hook echoes are drops.
ways: Hook is often 2 to 5 miles long.
Hook plus low CC means debris.

ex.q: What does a hook echo on reflectivity wrap around?

torn-L2#1.trap: Thinking the hook is the tornado. The tornado is near its tip.

torn-L2#2.why: A tornado vortex signature (TVS) shows on velocity radar as strong inbound (green) winds right beside strong outbound (red) winds. Next to each other means air is spinning tightly. It is a sign of intense rotation.
torn-L2#2.pic: Draw a radar dot. Draw a tiny green blob touching a tiny red blob. Draw a circle arrow around them.
torn-L2#2.analogy: A merry-go-round seen from the side: one edge comes toward you, the other goes away. It stops working because radar sees only one slice.
ways: A pair like -50 kt and +50 kt side by side is 100 kt of shear.

ex.q: On Doppler velocity radar, a tight pair of inbound and outbound winds next to each other shows what?

torn-L2#3.why: When a tornado lifts debris, the radar pulse hits many odd shapes: boards, leaves, dirt. They do not look alike, so correlation coefficient falls. A low CC spot inside the hook is a debris ball. It means the tornado is on the ground doing damage.
torn-L2#3.pic: Draw the hook echo with a small blue-colored dot at the tip labeled low CC.
torn-L2#3.analogy: A bag of mixed candy compared with a bag of identical candy. It stops working because candy is not flying.
ways: Rain CC about 0.98. Debris often below 0.8.
Low CC in a hook is a debris signature.

ex.q: Why does correlation coefficient drop inside a debris ball?
steps: Answer: debris targets are mixed in size and shape.

torn-L2#3.trap: Thinking low CC means light rain.

tstorm-L1#0.why: The National Weather Service calls a thunderstorm severe if it makes hail 1 inch or bigger, wind 58 mph or more, or a tornado. These thresholds mark damage: 1-inch hail dents cars and 58 mph wind breaks branches. Heavy rain or lightning alone do not make a storm severe.
tstorm-L1#0.pic: Draw a quarter, a gust arrow marked 58, and a funnel. Label them 'any one'.
tstorm-L1#0.analogy: A speeding ticket: you cross a line and it counts. It stops working because storms are not tickets.

ex.q: NWS criteria for a severe thunderstorm include hail at least how big?

tstorm-L1#1.why: A single-cell storm has one updraft. Rain forms, falls, and drags air down. The downdraft cuts off the warm updraft, so it dies in about an hour. With weak shear, rain falls into the updraft and kills it.
tstorm-L1#1.pic: Draw a cell with an up arrow, then a rain shaft over the arrow, then fading.
tstorm-L1#1.analogy: A candle with a cup placed over it. It stops working because storms are bigger.

ex.q: Why does a single-cell pulse storm die in about an hour?
steps: Answer: its downdraft cuts off the updraft.

tstorm-L1#1.trap: Thinking they run out of water.

tstorm-L1#2.why: A multicell cluster has many cells at different stages. Outflow from old cells lifts air to start new cells. So the group lasts for hours even if each cell dies in an hour. Lines of cells can bring wind and flooding.
tstorm-L1#2.pic: Draw three storms side by side: young, mature, old.
tstorm-L1#2.analogy: A relay race: runners change but the team keeps going. It stops working because cells are not people.
ways: Each cell about 1 hour, cluster several hours.

ex.q: A cluster of cells at different stages that keep forming new storms is what?

tstorm-L2#0.why: A supercell has one long-lived rotating updraft called a mesocyclone. Shear separates the updraft from the downdraft, so the storm keeps running. The rotation makes it capable of large hail and the strongest tornadoes.
tstorm-L2#0.pic: Draw a tilted giant cloud with a swirl in the middle labeled mesocyclone.
tstorm-L2#0.analogy: A hurricane in miniature. It stops working because they form differently.

ex.q: A very strong, long-lived thunderstorm forms with a rotating updraft. Which is most likely to produce a strong tornado?

tstorm-L2#0.trap: Thinking MCC makes the strongest tornadoes.

tstorm-L2#1.why: An MCC (mesoscale convective complex) is a huge, round cluster of storms. It forms at night over the Plains, can last 12 hours, and brings heavy rain. It is organized and has a big cold cloud shield on satellite.
tstorm-L2#1.pic: Draw a big round cold cloud on a satellite.
tstorm-L2#1.analogy: A big family reunion. It stops working because storms leave.
ways: Area over 100,000 sq km, lasting 6 hours or more.

ex.q: A large, long-lived, organized cluster of thunderstorms covering a big area is what?

tstorm-L2#2.why: A thunderstorm has three stages. Cumulus: updraft only, cloud grows. Mature: updraft and downdraft side by side, the worst weather. Dissipating: downdraft only, the storm fades. The downdraft cuts the supply.
tstorm-L2#2.pic: Draw three clouds: up arrows only, up and down arrows, down arrows only.
tstorm-L2#2.analogy: A life: growing, adult, retired. It stops working because storms don't age by years.

ex.q: Which stage has both an updraft and a downdraft?

upper-L1#0.why: Weather charts at fixed pressure levels show different jobs. 850 mb is about 1.5 km up and shows low-level moisture. 700 mb is about 3 km and shows steering. 500 mb is about 5.5 km and shows troughs and ridges. 300 mb is about 9 km and shows the jet stream. Pressure drops as you go up.
upper-L1#0.pic: Draw a vertical line with four marks: 850, 700, 500, 300. Label each job.
upper-L1#0.analogy: Floors of a building, each with a different job. It stops working because floors are fixed in height.
ways: 850 mb about 1.5 km, 700 about 3 km, 500 about 5.5 km, 300 about 9 km.

ex.q: Which pressure level is usually used to locate the jet stream?

upper-L1#1.why: A hodograph plots the wind at each height as a point on a graph, joined by a line. A long path means the wind changes a lot with height, so shear is strong. A clockwise curve helps supercells because it supports rotating updrafts.
upper-L1#1.pic: Draw axes. Plot dots at increasing height, join them in a curve going clockwise.
upper-L1#1.analogy: A map of a hike: a long winding path means a lot of change. It stops working because wind has direction too.
ways: Wind 10 kt at surface to 60 kt aloft is 50 kt change.

ex.q: Why does a long path on a hodograph mean strong shear?
steps: Each point is wind at a height.
Answer: wind changes a lot with height.

upper-L1#1.trap: Thinking a short path is bad.

upper-L1#2.why: A sounding is a balloon's profile of the air. Temperature is a solid line and dew point is a dashed line. Where the lines are close, the air is moist or cloudy. Where they are far apart, the air is dry.
upper-L1#2.pic: Draw two lines on a chart, close together at one level and far apart at another.
upper-L1#2.analogy: Two friends walking: close together means they are alike. It stops working because air isn't friendly.
ways: Close is moist, far is dry.
T 20, Td 19 is saturated-ish. T 20, Td 0 is dry.

ex.q: On a sounding, a wide gap between temperature and dew point means the layer is what?

upper-L2#0.why: An inversion is a layer where temperature rises with height, the opposite of normal. A warm layer on top of cooler air means rising parcels become cooler than their surroundings and stop. It is very stable, so it can cap storms. If the cap breaks, storms explode.
upper-L2#0.pic: Draw a temperature line going up, then bending to the right for a short stretch.
upper-L2#0.analogy: A lid on a pot. It stops working because the cap can leak.
ways: Temperature rises 22 C at 900 m to 25 C at 1000 m.

ex.q: A sounding layer where temperature increases with height is called what?

upper-L2#1.why: A Skew-T uses the same data as a Stüve. The temperature lines are tilted to the right to spread out the data and make the plots easier to read. So the skills are the same.
upper-L2#1.pic: Draw a square grid, then tilt its lines.
upper-L2#1.analogy: Like looking at a poster from an angle. It stops working because tilt changes shape.

ex.q: Skew-T diagrams differ from Stüve diagrams mainly because what?
steps: Answer: its temperature lines are tilted.

upper-L2#2.why: The LCL is the height where a rising parcel becomes saturated and forms cloud. The gap between temperature and dew point tells how far it must rise. About 125 m for every degree C of gap. A lower LCL means a lower cloud base, which favors tornadoes.
upper-L2#2.pic: Draw a parcel rising from the ground to a cloud base at the LCL.
upper-L2#2.analogy: Like a balloon cooling until it fogs. It stops working because it is an approximation.

ex.q: Surface temperature is 30 C and dew point is 18 C. What is the LCL?

upper-L2#3.why: CAPE is the energy stored for storms, in joules per kilogram. It measures how much a rising parcel would speed up. Under 1000 is marginal, 1000 to 2500 moderate, 2500 to 4000 strong, over 4000 extreme.
upper-L2#3.pic: Draw a sounding with a shaded area between parcel and environment.
upper-L2#3.analogy: A fuel tank gauge. It stops working because CAPE is not used up.

ex.q: CAPE of 300 J/kg is best described as what?

upper-L2#3.trap: Thinking CAPE alone makes a storm.
upper-L2#3.tip: CAPE is cake: more is stronger.

winds-L1#0.why: Thunderstorm winds come from two sources: rotation (a tornado) or air that rushes straight along the ground. Straight-line wind is the second kind. Rain-cooled air is heavy, so it sinks, hits the ground, and spreads out in a line. The damage path points the same way, like a bowling lane. Tornado damage instead twists and swirls around a center. Straight-line wind is the most common storm wind report because every strong storm can make it, but only a few make tornadoes.
winds-L1#0.pic: Draw a storm cloud. Under it, draw arrows going down, then bending flat along the ground in one direction. Draw trees all lying with their tops pointing the same way.
winds-L1#0.analogy: Think of a glass of water dumped on a table. The water hits and spreads out in all directions in a line from the splash. The storm's cold air is the water, the ground is the table. Unlike a spill, the storm wind can be 60 to 100 mph and last minutes.
ways: Wind damage with no spin is straight-line wind.
Fallen trees: 10 pointing east, 0 pointing other ways = straight-line. Trees pointing every direction in a small spot = rotation.
Same direction means straight-line. Swirly means tornado.

ex.q: A neighborhood has 12 fallen trees, all pointing north-east, and no rotation seen on radar. What caused it?
steps: Look at the tree directions: all the same way.
Same direction means the wind pushed in one straight path.
No rotation on radar rules out a tornado.
Rain-cooled air sank and spread out along the ground.

winds-L1#0.trap: Thinking any storm wind damage is a tornado. Check the pattern: parallel means straight-line, twisted means tornado.
winds-L1#0.tip: Straight trees fall in a straight line: straight-line wind.

winds-L1#1.why: A downburst starts when rain and hail drag air down inside a storm. Falling rain also cools the air as water evaporates, which makes it denser than the air around it. Dense air sinks fast. When it hits the ground it cannot go further down, so it fans out sideways in all directions. That outward burst is what knocks things over. Without the ground to stop it, it would just keep falling and there would be no sideways blast.
winds-L1#1.pic: Draw a storm cloud. Below it draw a thick arrow pointing down. At the ground, draw arrows curving out to the left and right like a starburst. Label the spot 'impact'.
winds-L1#1.analogy: A water balloon dropped on the floor: the water falls down, hits, then splashes out sideways. The downdraft is the falling balloon, the ground is the floor, the spreading outflow is the splash. A real downburst can be invisible when the air is dry and no rain reaches the ground.
ways: A downdraft that hits the ground and spreads out is a downburst.
Air goes down at maybe 30 mph, then spreads outward at 60+ mph near the ground.
Side view: arrow down, then arrows flat in both directions along the ground.

ex.q: A downdraft hits the ground and winds spread outward. What is it called?
steps: Notice the air goes down first.
Then it spreads outward in all directions.
That full pattern defines a downburst.

winds-L1#1.trap: Mixing it up with a tornado. A tornado rotates and pulls inward; a downburst blows outward.

winds-L1#2.why: Size is the only difference between the two. A microburst is a small downburst, under 4 km wide. The small size makes the wind very strong in a tiny area and it can last just a few minutes. A macroburst is 4 km or more wide and can last longer. The word micro means small and macro means large, so you can remember the sizes from the Greek parts of the words.
winds-L1#2.pic: Draw a circle 4 km wide on a grid. Draw a small circle inside it for a microburst and a big one reaching past it for a macroburst. Label the line '4 km'.
winds-L1#2.analogy: A sprinkler head versus a fire hose: both spray water out, but one covers a small patch and one covers a big area. Microburst is the small spray, macroburst the big one. Real winds differ in strength too, not just size.
ways: Under 4 km is micro. 4 km or more is macro.
3 km wide = microburst. 4 km wide = macroburst. 10 km wide = macroburst.
Four kilometers is the dividing line.

ex.q: A downburst spreads over an area 7 km wide. Micro or macro?
steps: Compare 7 km with the 4 km cutoff.
Four or more km means macroburst.

winds-L1#2.trap: Calling exactly 4 km a microburst. The rule says 4 km or more is macro.
winds-L1#2.tip: Micro is mini; macro is massive.

winds-L2#0.why: Rain-cooled air sinks and spreads out under a storm. The edge of this cool pool is the gust front. It pushes into the warm air in front of the storm like a snow plow. Warm air is lifted by the cool wedge. When the lifted air cools enough, a cloud forms along the edge. That low, wedge-shaped cloud is the shelf cloud. The gust front arrives before the rain, so a sudden wind shift and temperature drop tells you a storm is near.
winds-L2#0.pic: Draw the ground and a storm on the right. Draw a low blob of cool air with a sloping front edge. Draw an arrow of warm air rising over the slope and a shelf cloud on top of the edge.
winds-L2#0.analogy: A snow plow pushes snow ahead of it. The cool outflow is the plow, warm air is the snow being shoved up. The plow stops pushing when it runs out of power, and a gust front fades the same way.
ways: Gust front: leading edge of cool outflow. Shelf cloud: wedge cloud on top of it.
Before: 90 F, calm. At front: wind jumps to 50 mph, temperature falls to 75 F.
Wind and cool air arrive first; the rain follows.

ex.q: A low, wedge-shaped cloud sits on the front edge of a storm. What is it?
steps: Notice the cloud is low and wedge-shaped.
It sits at the front edge of outflow.
Warm air lifted by the gust front makes it.
That cloud type is a shelf cloud.

winds-L2#0.trap: Confusing a shelf cloud with a wall cloud. Shelf clouds are on the front edge and spread wide; wall clouds hang lower under the storm base and can rotate.
winds-L2#0.tip: Shelf cloud: a shelf over the front.

winds-L2#1.why: A squall line is a row of storms that formed in a line. When the storms push cool air out in one strong, shared surge, the line can race ahead. The line can bend into a bow shape. The strongest wind blows from the middle of the bow. If the line lasts a long time and causes damage over hundreds of miles, it is called a derecho. A derecho keeps going because its cool outflow keeps lifting new warm air, which feeds new storms.
winds-L2#1.pic: Draw a long line of storm cells across a map from left to right. Bend the middle forward into a bow. Draw arrows pointing straight out from the middle and a long damage path trailing behind.
winds-L2#1.analogy: A line of dominoes: one falling hits the next, so the whole row keeps going. Each storm is a domino pushing air that triggers the next. A derecho is a very long row that keeps falling for hours. Dominoes run out of row; storms run out of warm, moist air.
ways: Squall line: storms in a line. Derecho: long-lived, wide windstorm.
Damage swath of 400+ miles and wind gusts of 58 mph or more are signs of a derecho.
A squall line is the group. A derecho is the extreme version.

ex.q: A fast-moving band of storms damages trees across 450 miles with winds over 60 mph. Name it.
steps: The storms move as a band.
The damage is long: 450 miles, in the hundreds.
The wind is strong and straight-line.
A long-lived windstorm like this is a derecho.

winds-L2#1.trap: Thinking every squall line is a derecho. Most are not; a derecho needs a long path of damage.

winds-L2#2.why: Downslope wind needs no storm. Air flows over a mountain, then sinks down the far side. Sinking air gets squeezed by higher pressure, which heats it. It warms by about 5.5 F for every 1,000 ft it drops when dry. Gravity and a pressure difference speed it up as it goes down the slope. In a thunderstorm downdraft, air is heavy from rain and cool from evaporation, so gravity pulls it quickly toward the ground.
winds-L2#2.pic: Draw a mountain. Draw arrows rising up the left side and plunging down the right side, getting longer as they go. Label the bottom 'warm, dry, gusty'.
winds-L2#2.analogy: A kid sliding down a playground slide speeds up as they go. The air is the kid, the slope is the slide. Unlike a slide, air also warms as it descends.
ways: Air sinking down a mountain speeds up and warms.
Drop 3,000 ft: dry air warms about 16.5 F (3 x 5.5).
Heavier or colder than surroundings means it sinks fast.

ex.q: Dry air drops 2,000 ft down a slope. About how much does it warm at 5.5 F per 1,000 ft?
steps: Drop is 2,000 ft, which is 2 thousands.

winds-L2#2.trap: Saying you need a thunderstorm for strong sinking wind. Mountains alone can do it.
winds-L2#2.tip: Down the slope, speed and warm both grow.

winds-L2#3.why: Radar sees rain and hail, not wind. But wind shapes where the rain goes. When a squall line surges forward in the middle, radar shows a bow-shaped echo. That bow means fast winds pushing the line ahead, so the middle is the most damaging. A fine line is a thin streak where outflow lifts air and dust or bugs; it marks a gust front. Learn the shape and you can guess the wind.
winds-L2#3.pic: Draw a straight line on a radar screen, then the same line with its middle bulged forward like an archer's bow. Mark the strongest wind at the bulge. Draw a thin dotted line ahead of storms and label it gust front.
winds-L2#3.analogy: A rope held by two people: if the middle is pushed, it bows out. The storm line is the rope, the fast wind is the push. Unlike rope, the radar bow is formed by air, not a hand.
ways: Bow echo means strong wind. Fine line means gust front.
Bowing segment gusts: often 60 to 80 mph. Other parts of line: weaker.
Straight line = normal. Bowed line = strong wind.

ex.q: On radar a line of storms bows out in the middle. Where is the wind strongest?
steps: Find the bowing part of the line.
The outward push is where air is fastest.
So winds are strongest at the bow.

winds-L2#3.trap: Looking only at color. The shape of the echo tells you about wind.

winter-L1#0.why: A blizzard is about wind and visibility, not how much snow falls. Needed: wind or gusts of 35 mph or more, snow in the air, and visibility under 1/4 mile, for at least 3 hours. Wind picks up snow and fills the air, making a whiteout. Without strong wind, snow falls straight down and you can see further. All three parts must happen together for 3 hours.
winter-L1#0.pic: Draw a road with flat white ground. Add a wind arrow marked 35 mph. Draw snow filling the air so a car 1/4 mile away disappears. Put a clock showing 3 hours.
winter-L1#0.analogy: A snow globe: shake it and you cannot see through. The wind is the shake. The globe stops swirling after a moment, but a blizzard keeps going for hours.
ways: Strong wind + snow in air + low visibility, for 3 hours.
40 mph wind, 1/8 mile visibility, 4 hours = blizzard. 25 mph, 1/8 mile, 4 hours = not.

ex.q: Wind gusts 38 mph, visibility 1/8 mile in blowing snow, for 4 hours. Blizzard?
steps: Time of 4 hours is at least 3.

winter-L1#0.trap: Thinking heavy snow makes a blizzard. A light snowfall with strong wind can qualify; heavy snow with calm wind cannot.

winter-L1#1.why: Blowing snow counts. Wind can lift old snow off the ground and fill the air. That drops visibility the same as new snow. So the test only asks for wind, snow in the air, and low visibility. It does not care where the snow came from. A clear, sunny sky can still have a ground blizzard.
winter-L1#1.pic: Draw a sunny sky with no clouds. On the ground draw wind arrows kicking up a cloud of old snow. Label it 'ground blizzard'.
winter-L1#1.analogy: A broom sweeping dust: the dust was already there but it fills the air. Wind is the broom and old snow is the dust. The broom can't sweep up more than is there; if the ground is bare, no blizzard.
ways: Old snow blown by wind can meet the blizzard test.
0 inches of new snow, 40 mph wind, visibility 1/8 mile for 3 hours: still a blizzard.
Needed: wind, snow in air, low view. Not needed: new snow.

ex.q: Which is NOT required for a blizzard: wind, low visibility, or new snowfall?
steps: List the required items: wind, snow in air, low visibility.
Check each option against the list.
New snowfall is not on the list.

winter-L1#1.trap: Believing it must be snowing. It does not have to be.

winter-L1#2.why: A nor'easter is a big storm along the East Coast with winds from the northeast. The winds push ocean water toward the coast for days. Water piles up, and slow-moving storms mean it lasts through several high tides. Each high tide sits on the extra water, so flooding repeats. Add heavy snow or rain and strong gusts, and it is a major event.
winter-L1#2.pic: Draw the East Coast on the right and ocean on the left. Draw a low-pressure circle offshore with wind arrows from the northeast toward the coast. Show water piled against shore.
winter-L1#2.analogy: A bathtub being pushed by a hand: pushing water to one end raises it there. Wind is the hand, the coast the tub end. Unlike a tub, tides rise and fall on top, so flooding comes in waves.
ways: Northeast winds, big storm, snow, wind, coastal floods.
Normal high tide plus 3 ft storm surge = flooding at each high tide for 2 days.
Slow storm plus repeated high tides means long flooding.

ex.q: Storm surge adds 3 ft for 3 days at 2 high tides per day. How many high tides are affected?

winter-L1#2.trap: Thinking the flooding ends after the first high tide. A slow storm keeps pushing water.
winter-L1#2.tip: Nor'easter: wind from the northeast, tides keep the flood.

winter-L2#0.why: Cold air moves over warm open lake water. The lake heats and moistens the bottom of the air. Warm moist air rises, forms clouds, and drops snow. Wind carries the snow downwind so it falls in narrow bands along the shore. The bigger the temperature difference between lake and air, the heavier the snow. If the lake freezes, the supply stops.
winter-L2#0.pic: Draw a lake with wind arrows blowing across it. Draw wavy arrows rising off the water and a thick cloud band downwind. Shade the shore underneath with heavy snow.
winter-L2#0.analogy: A pot of hot water in a cold room: steam rises off the top. The lake is the pot, cold air is the room. The pot cools if you don't reheat it, but a big lake stays warm for weeks.
ways: Cold air plus warm lake equals snow bands downwind.
Lake 45 F, air 15 F: difference 30 F. Bigger difference, more snow.
Needs open water that is warmer than the air.

ex.q: Lake water is 40 F and air is 10 F. What is the difference?
steps: Answer: 30 F; a large difference, good for snow.

winter-L2#0.trap: Thinking it snows everywhere equally. It falls in narrow bands downwind.
winter-L2#0.tip: Warm lake, cold air: snow over there.

winter-L2#1.why: Freezing rain falls as liquid, then freezes on contact with surfaces below 32 F. It coats lines, trees, and roads with a layer of ice. Even 1/4 inch can add hundreds of pounds to a power line and break branches. Sleet bounces and does not stick, so it builds little weight. That is why freezing rain is worse for power lines. A cold layer near the ground freezes the drops on touching.
winter-L2#1.pic: Draw a power line with a thick tube of ice around it. Draw raindrops falling and freezing where they touch. Draw a sleeping tree branch bending under the ice.
winter-L2#1.analogy: A glaze on a donut: liquid sugar coats the donut and hardens. Freezing rain is the glaze, objects are the donut. The glaze is sweet; ice is dangerous.
ways: Freezing rain coats everything with ice.
1/4 inch of ice on lines can bring down trees and wires.

ex.q: Which builds heavier ice on power lines: sleet or freezing rain?
steps: Sleet is ice pellets that bounce.
Freezing rain stays liquid until it touches.
It then spreads and freezes in a layer.

winter-L2#1.trap: Thinking sleet and freezing rain are the same. Sleet bounces, freezing rain coats.
